newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sumitomo shareholder plans suit over copper losses.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo shareholder plans suit over copper losses.

text.p: A Sumitomo Corp shareholder notified the company on Monday he will sue its directors for compensation because of the company's massive copper trading losses, one of his lawyers said.

In a notice submitted to Sumitomo, Kazuyoshi Yuoka asked the auditor to file suit against directors from the company for not properly supervising former copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka as he allegedly racked up a $2.6 billion loss from unauthorised trades over a 10-year period.

Under Japanese law, if the auditor does not file suit within 30 days, the shareholder may then sue the company on his own. The suit would require the directors to compensate the company as a whole rather than just the shareholder who files suit.

Tadashi Matsumaru, a lawyer for Yuoka, said it had not been decided whether the suit would request compensation for the entire $2.6 billion loss. He also said the suit may target only those directors considered directly responsible for the losses.

Yuoka, who owns 2,000 of Sumitomo's more than one billion shares, also filed a suit against the company in late September to repeal last June's shareholder approval of a fund to cover the copper losses.
A Sumitomo spokesman declined to comment on Yuoka's latest move, saying the company was still studying the notification.
Sumitomo officials have repeatedly said that its massive losses, first announced in June, were due solely to Hamanaka's secret deals and that his superiors were kept in the dark.

Hamanaka was recently arrested for fraud and forgery in connection with the unauthorised trading. One of his lawyers has said Hamanaka has admitted to the forgery charges but that he has not commented directly on whether any of his bosses knew of his losing trades.
The statement Yuoka submitted to Sumitomo today charged that the directors did not fulfil their responsibility to supervise copper transactions and ensure there were no improprieties.

The statement said, for example, that if Sumitomo's directors had carried out investigations and supervision in response to inquiries from the London Metal Exchange in 1991, when a U.S. trader accused Hamanaka of asking for verification of phony trades, they should have been able to discover Hamanaka's improper actions.
